passage:
Last Diwali I refused to do the puja with everyone. I told Dadi I didn't see why lighting a lamp mattered if I wasn't sure I believed in it. I'd spent the week on old punk songs and a library book about Stoic philosophers, so I felt very grown up. My cousin Jatin, who loves a debate, told me to argue the other side, just for fun. So I did: the lamp as a way of saying the family is together, the ritual as a pause in a loud year. Halfway through, he grinned, because I'd started half-believing my own case. That annoyed me. I'd thought saying no was the same as thinking for myself. Now I think it was only saying no. This year I might light the lamp and keep asking my questions.
Alka

qa.q: What had Alka spent the week listening to?
qa.a: Alka had spent the week on old punk songs.

qa.q: Why was Alka annoyed halfway through the argument?
qa.a: Alka started half-believing the case for the lamp, which shook the idea that refusing was the same as thinking independently.

qa.q: What choice does Alka make about this year's Diwali?
qa.a: Alka plans to light the lamp and keep asking questions, joining in without giving up independent thought.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Alka refused the puja?
qa.a: Dadi may have felt hurt or worried that the family ritual was being rejected, even though Alka meant it as a question.

grounding: A teenager questions a family custom, tries new music and philosophy, argues both sides, and sees that refusing tradition is not the same as independence.

passage:
Debate club notes, Friday. Vandana, club mentor
Mehak, Class 10, argued for school uniforms in the first round and against them in the second, and was sharper both times. She grinned when nobody could tell which side she really held. Afterwards she played me a clip of throat singing she has just discovered and asked why our assembly songs never change. Then she said, a bit too proudly, that she had skipped her cousin's engagement "because traditions are for sheep." I asked which part she actually disliked, the ceremony or being told to go. She went quiet, then said, "Being told, I think." We agreed she will write next week's motion on choosing traditions rather than just refusing them. Her energy is a gift, and I want to keep giving it room.

qa.q: What did Mehak argue for in the first round?
qa.a: Mehak argued for school uniforms in the first round.

qa.q: What does Mehak's quiet pause after Vandana's question suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She seems caught off guard and unsure as she rethinks; she sees that what she disliked was being told, not the engagement itself.

qa.q: What choice did Vandana make instead of lecturing Mehak about the engagement?
qa.a: Vandana asked what she really disliked and then offered her a debate motion, turning a proud remark into real thinking.

qa.q: How might Mehak's cousin see her skipping the engagement?
qa.a: The cousin may feel hurt or left out, taking it as a rejection of them rather than of a custom.

grounding: A teenager enjoys arguing both sides and new music, and a mentor helps her notice she has mixed up refusing tradition with being independent.

passage: At the Lunar New Year dinner in Vancouver, Xin refused to bow to the ancestors' photographs. 'Why should I honour people I never met, just because we always have?' Grandma put her chopsticks down and said nothing. The next morning, walking to school, Xin argued the opposite to Freya: 'Actually it's kind of beautiful, remembering people on purpose.' Freya laughed. 'Last night you said it was pointless.' 'I'm testing the idea.' All month Xin had been living on punk records, a philosophy podcast and a notebook of quotes, feeling more awake than ever. 'So which do you actually believe?' Freya asked. Xin didn't answer. Refusing had felt like being free. Now it looked a bit like just another rule, only backwards.

qa.q: What did Xin refuse to do at the Lunar New Year dinner?
qa.a: Xin refused to bow to the ancestors' photographs.

qa.q: Why did Xin go quiet when Freya asked which view Xin believed?
qa.a: Xin felt unsure and a little confused, beginning to see that refusing the custom had felt like freedom without being a real choice.

qa.q: What could Xin do before the next family dinner?
qa.a: Xin could ask Grandma what bowing means to her and then decide what to keep, rather than rejecting it just to feel independent.

qa.q: How might Grandma have felt when Xin refused?
qa.a: Grandma was likely hurt or shocked, putting her chopsticks down in silence, as a custom honouring family was dismissed at the table.

grounding: Shows a teenager questioning a family custom, trying new music and ideas, enjoying arguing both sides, and wondering whether refusal is really independence.

passage: In the debate club room of her Bengaluru school, Sabina was arguing, hands flying, that traditions survive only because nobody dares question them. Ten minutes later she asked Ms. Kulkarni if she could argue the other side. 'You can't do both,' Nandini said. 'Watch me.' And she did: festivals as memory, recipes as maps of who we were. The room clapped. Afterwards, packing up, Nandini tapped the small gold stud in Sabina's nose. 'You wear your nani's nose pin every day, and you just called tradition a cage.' Sabina touched it. She'd spent the month reading about existentialism, listening to Sufi rock, cutting her hair short. Throwing everything out had felt like growing up. Now she wasn't sure what she was throwing, or why.

qa.q: Whose nose pin does Sabina wear every day?
qa.a: Her nani's.

qa.q: What does Sabina touching the nose pin suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She feels caught out and unsure, realising she keeps a tradition she loves even while calling tradition a cage.

qa.q: What could Sabina ask herself before rejecting a custom?
qa.a: Whether she is questioning it for what it means or only because it is old, and which parts, like the nose pin, she actually wants to keep.

qa.q: Why might Nandini have pointed out the nose pin?
qa.a: Nandini may have felt Sabina's big claims didn't match her life, and wanted to nudge her to think harder rather than just win.

grounding: Shows a teenager who loves arguing both sides and trying new ideas, and starts to notice she may be mistaking rejecting tradition for independence.

passage:
Dear Devika Didi,
You said to write when things got weird, so: things are weird. This month I've read half a book on free will, found a jazz station that plays till two in the morning, and told Papa at dinner that our yearly trip to the village temple is 'just habit dressed up as meaning'. He went quiet. The next evening, partly to annoy him, I argued the opposite, that habits are how families remember. I loved both arguments. I felt awake in a way school never makes me feel.
But here's the weird part. I said I'm not going this year, and now I don't know if that's because I've thought it through, or because saying no feels like being my own person. How did you know which of your changes were really yours?
Ujjwal

qa.q: What did Ujjwal tell Papa about the yearly temple trip?
qa.a: That it is 'just habit dressed up as meaning'.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal feel about all these new ideas?
qa.a: Ujjwal feels awake and excited by them, but also unsure whether refusing the trip is a real choice or just a way to feel independent.

qa.q: What might help Ujjwal decide about the temple trip?
qa.a: Talking calmly with Papa or Devika about what the trip means to the family, and only then deciding whether to go.

qa.q: What might Papa have felt when he went quiet at dinner?
qa.a: Papa may have felt hurt or unsettled to hear a family custom called empty, and unsure how to reply.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring new music and philosophy, enjoying arguing both sides, and unsure whether rejecting a family custom is true independence.

passage: Pranav, you asked why I wore black to Riya Didi's haldi last year. Honestly? I was fifteen and I wanted to reject everything. I'm Jyoti, and that year I listened only to heavy metal, read philosophy books I half understood, and told Dadaji over dinner that rituals were superstition. I loved arguing. I'd argue for God one night and against God the next, just to see where the idea went. It felt electric, like my brain was growing. But at the haldi, everyone was laughing and dancing, and I sat in a corner in black, proving a point nobody cared about. That's when I realised saying no to everything wasn't the same as thinking for myself. Now I choose. I still argue with Dadaji. But I sang at Diwali, because I wanted to.

qa.q: What colour did Jyoti wear to the haldi?
qa.a: Black.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when arguing both sides of big questions?
qa.a: Jyoti felt electric and alive, as if the mind was growing.

qa.q: What did Jyoti learn at the haldi?
qa.a: That rejecting everything was not the same as independent thinking, so Jyoti now chooses what to keep, like singing at Diwali.

qa.q: How might Dadaji have felt about the dinner-table arguments?
qa.a: Dadaji may have felt challenged and perhaps hurt at first, but also engaged, since they still argue now.

grounding: Shows a teenager questioning customs and trying new music and philosophies, enjoying arguing both sides, and realising rejecting tradition isn't the same as independence.
